questions.problem:
$$

Consider the curve ${x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y=3.$ Given that $x=x(t),\text{ }y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=7$ on the curve at the point $(1,3),$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=7,$ $x=1,$ and $y=3,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 7\cdot (2(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1))+(1)^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{1}\cdot 7+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 0+7+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 7+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the parabola $3{y}^{2}-4x=0.$ Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ on the curve at the point $(3,2),$ find the value of  $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}-4x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{y}^{2}-4x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(3{y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (6y)-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6,$ $x=3,$ and $y=2,$ and solve $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ We get  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (6(2))-(6)\cdot 4 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (12)-24 & =0 \\ 12\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =24 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$

Consider the curve $x\operatorname{cos}⁡y=2.$ Given that $x=x(t),\text{ }y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ on the curve at the point $(4,\frac{\pi }{3}),$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point. Do not round the answer.

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6,$ $x=4,$ and $y=\frac{\pi }{3},$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y-x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 6\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 6\cdot \frac{1}{2}-4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ 3-2\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-16x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}-16x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(16x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(16x) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y)-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{4},$ $x=1,$ and $y=4,$ and solving for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y)-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 16 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2\cdot 4)-(\frac{1}{4})\cdot 16 & =0 \\ 8\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-4 & =0 \\ 8\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2}=1.$ Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ on the curve at the point $(2\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3}),$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6,$ $x=2\sqrt{3},$ and $y=\sqrt{3},$ and solve $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ We get  

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot (\frac{2(2\sqrt{3})}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2(\sqrt{3})) & =0 \\ -2\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-8\sqrt{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using an Implicitly Defined Curve to Determine a Second Coordinate
questions.problem: Consider the curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-{y}^{3}=-8.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{12}$ on the curve at the point where $x=1,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-{y}^{3} & =-8 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-8) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{3}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}))-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{3}{x})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (3{y}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{12}$ and $x=1.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-{y}^{3} & =-8 \\ 0-{y}^{3} & =-8 \\ {y}^{3} & =8 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3-\frac{1}{4}(2)^{2} & =0 \\ 3\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve $\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)=2.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2$ on the curve at the point where $x=\frac{1}{2},$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{1}{y}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2$ and $x=\frac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{1}{y}) & =0 \\ -8+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{1}{y}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=\frac{1}{2}$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=\frac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ 2+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}-8+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (1) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-8{e}^{x}-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}-8{e}^{x}-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{e}^{x})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(8\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2y-\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8{e}^{x}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{8}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ and $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-48{e}^{x}-8\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =0 \\ -6\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-48{e}^{x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $y=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-8{e}^{x}-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =0 \\ {1}^{2}-8{e}^{x}-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & =0 \\ 1-8{e}^{x}-0 & =0 \\ -8{e}^{x} & =-1 \\ {e}^{x} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-6\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-48{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})} & =0 \\ -6\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =48\cdot \frac{1}{8} \\ -6\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =6 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{6}{-6} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve ${x}^{2}+{e}^{y}=5.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1$ on the curve at the point where $x=-2,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{e}^{y} & =5 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{y}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({e}^{y}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $x=-2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=-2$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{e}^{y} & =5 \\ 4+{e}^{y} & =5 \\ {e}^{y} & =1 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot {e}^{0} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the curve ${e}^{x-2}+2{y}^{2}=3.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{2}$ on the curve at the point where $y=1,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-2}+2{y}^{2} & =3 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x-2}+2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{x-2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x-2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{x-2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (4y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{2}$ and $y=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{x-2})+\frac{3}{2}\cdot (4) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{x-2})+6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $y=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-2}+2{y}^{2} & =3 \\ {e}^{x-2}+2 & =3 \\ {e}^{x-2} & =1 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, substituting $x=2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot ({e}^{2-2})+6 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the section of the parabola ${x}^{2}-4y=4$ that lies in the first quadrant.  Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=3$ on the parabola at the point where $y=3,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4y & =4 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}-4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(4y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $y=3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)-(3)\cdot 4 & =0 \\ 2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-12 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=3$ into the equation of  the parabola.  

At the point where $y=3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4y & =4 \\ {x}^{2}-4\cdot (3) & =4 \\ {x}^{2}-12 & =4 \\ {x}^{2} & =16 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $x>0$ since we're only interested in the  first  quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $x=4,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-12 & =0 \\ 8\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =12 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{12}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the section of the hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1$ that lies in the second quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4$ on the hyperbola at the point where $x=-3,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4$ and $x=-3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (-2)-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0 \\ -8-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=-3$ into the equation of the hyperbola.

At the point where $x=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(-3)^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ 3-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the second quadrant.

 Finally, substituting $y=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the section of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ that lies in the second quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt{3}$ on the circle at the point where $x=-\sqrt{3},$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt{3}$ and $x=-\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2\cdot (-\sqrt{3}))+(\sqrt{3})\cdot (2y) & =0. \\ -2\sqrt{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2\sqrt{3}y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =y.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=-\sqrt{3}$ into the equation of the circle.

At the point where $x=-\sqrt{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {(-\sqrt{3})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ 3+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the second 
quadrant.

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =y \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the section of the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}=1$ that lies in the first quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt{2}$ on the circle at the point where $x=1,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{y}{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt{2}$ and $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (1)+(\sqrt{2})\cdot (\frac{y}{2}) & =0. \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\sqrt{2}\text{ }\,y}{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=1$ into the equation of the ellipse. 

At the point where $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {y}^{2} & =2 \\ y & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y>0$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $y=\sqrt{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}}{2} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =169 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(169) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, substituting the given information $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=5$ and $y=12,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2x)+5\cdot (2(12)) & =0 \\ 2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+120 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $x,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $y=12$ into the equation of the circle.  

At the point where $y=12,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =169 \\ {x}^{2}+{12}^{2} & =169 \\ {x}^{2}+144 & =169 \\ {x}^{2} & =25 \\ x & =\pm 5.\end{aligned}
$$

We choose $x=5$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $x=5,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+120 & =0 \\ 2(5)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+120 & =0 \\ 10\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-120 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{-120}{10} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating a Related Rate From an Implicitly Defined Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following ellipse: 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=1
$$

 

Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=\sqrt{2}$ on the curve at the point $(1,\sqrt2),$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$ at that point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (x)+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{y}{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=\sqrt{2},$ $x=1,$ and $y=\sqrt2,$ and solve $\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$  We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (1)+\sqrt{2}\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+1 & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the curve $x^3-\ln y=1.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ on the curve at the point where $x=1,$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}$ at that point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3{x}^{2}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ and $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{1} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Using the Equation of a Conic Section to Determine a Second Coordinate
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the section of the hyperbola 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{3}-\dfrac{y^2}{2}=1
$$

that lies in the first quadrant. Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=-2$ on the hyperbola at the point where $x=3,$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}$ at this point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}=-2$ and $x=3.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2\cdot 3}{3})-(-2)\cdot y & =0 \\ 2\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-y.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We also want to substitute for $y$, but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=3$ into the equation of the hyperbola.   

At the point where $x=3,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{3}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used $y > 0$ since we're only interested in the first quadrant. 

Finally, substituting $y= 2,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-y \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$
